title: "Integral Calculus"
subtitle: "Accumulation, numerical integration, convergence, and gradient descent"

## Course Description

A second course in differential and integral calculus of a single variable: integration; techniques of integration; infinite sequences and series; polar and parametric equations; applications of integration.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Course Content

1.  Areas between curves;
2.  Volume, volume of a solid of revolution;
3.  Additional techniques of integration including integration by parts and trigonometric substitution;
4.  Numerical integration; trapezoidal and Simpson's rule;
5.  Improper integrals;
6.  Applications of integration to areas and volumes;
7.  Additional applications such as work, arc length, area of a surface of revolution, moments and centers of mass, separable differential equations, growth and decay;
8.  Introduction to sequences and series;
9.  Multiple tests for convergence of sequences and series; 
10. Power series, radius of convergence, interval of convergence;
11. Differentiation and integration of power series;
12. Taylor series expansion of functions;
13. Parametric equations and calculus with parametric curves; and
14. Polar curves and calculus in polar coordinates;
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Course Objectives
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

1.  Evaluate indeterminate forms using L'Hopital's Rule;
2.  Find derivatives of transcendental functions;
3.  Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals using a variety of integration formulas and techniques;
4.  Apply integration to areas and volumes, and other applications such as work or length of a curve;
5.  Evaluate improper integrals;
6.  Apply convergence tests to sequences and series;
7.  Represent functions as power series; and
8.  Graph, differentiate and integrate functions in polar and parametric form.
:::

## Connections to Data Science: Probability Theory and Convergence
Integral calculus helps us understand how quantities accumulate, which makes it useful for both probability and optimization. In gradient descent, ideas such as convexity and convergence can be introduced in a simple way: convex functions have a bowl-like shape, and when the steps are chosen appropriately, repeatedly moving downhill can bring us closer to a minimum. Integrals also allow us to find the total area under probability distributions, which must equal 1 because it represents the total probability. For example, exponential, Gamma, and Beta distributions can be integrated analytically to study probabilities and expected values. The normal distribution is different: its total area and probabilities cannot be expressed using an elementary antiderivative, so we approximate them numerically. This provides a natural connection between integration techniques and the numerical methods used in statistics, data science, and machine learning.
